topic: Tree Traversals, Properties, BST Operations, and Tree Construction

problems.title: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the inorder traversal of its nodes' values.

Input and output are represented in array format (inorder values for return).

parameterDefinitions.name: root
parameterDefinitions.description: Binary tree represented in level-order array

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: Inorder visit: left subtree (empty), root (1), right subtree (3 then 2).

problems.optimalSpaceComplexity: O(H) where H is tree height
commonMistakes: Confusing Inorder (Left, Root, Right) with Preorder (Root, Left, Right)
Not handling null root correctly
hints: Inorder traversal visits left subtree, then the root node, then the right subtree.
Can be implemented easily with recursion or an explicit stack.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

examples.explanation: Postorder visits left, right, then root.
Leaves 4 and 5 visited before 2, subtrees before root 1.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.statement: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values (i.e., from left to right, level by level).
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 2000].
commonMistakes: Not snapshotting queue.length before the inner loop, causing dynamic loop boundaries
Returning empty array inside array `[[]]` instead of `[]` for empty tree
hints: Use a FIFO queue for Breadth-First Search (BFS).
At the start of each level, record `const size = queue.length` to process exactly one level per iteration.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=255 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=127 for complexity verification

problems.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problems.statement: Given the `root` of a binary tree, imagine yourself standing on the right side of it, return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from top to bottom.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: Looking from right side: 1 on top, 3 in middle, 4 at bottom.
Node 4 on the left subtree is visible because right subtree does not extend to depth 3.

problems.optimalSpaceComplexity: O(D) where D is tree diameter
commonMistakes: Only traversing right children: if left subtree is deeper than right subtree, left nodes will be visible from the right
Returning the rightmost element in the array representation instead of the tree level
hints: Traverse level by level using BFS; the last node processed in each level is visible from the right side.
Alternatively, DFS visiting right child before left child; add to result when `depth === res.length`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.

A binary tree's maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^4].
problems.suboptimalSpaceComplexity: O(W) where W is max width
commonMistakes: Returning 1 instead of 0 for empty tree
Counting edges instead of nodes
hints: The maximum depth of a node is 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).
Base case: depth of null is 0.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=127 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=255 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.statement:
Given a binary tree, find its minimum depth.

The minimum depth is the number of nodes along the shortest path from the root node down to the nearest leaf node.

Note: A leaf is a node with no children.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^5].

examples.explanation: Shortest path to leaf 9 has length 2.
Only one branch, leaf is 6 at depth 5.
Node 1 has right null, but 1 is not a leaf; leaf is 2 at depth 2.

commonMistakes: Doing `1 + min(dfs(left), dfs(right))` directly: if one child is null, it returns 1, but a node with one child is NOT a leaf!
Confusing BFS level termination condition
hints: A leaf node must have both `left == null` and `right == null`.
BFS guarantees you find the shortest path to a leaf on the very first leaf encountered.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=127 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification

examples.explanation: Every left and right subtree swapped at each level.

commonMistakes: Overwriting `node.left` before passing its original value to `invert(node.right)`
Returning null instead of [] for empty input

problems.title: Same Tree
problems.statement:
Given the roots of two binary trees `p` and `q`, write a function to check if they are the same or not.

Two binary trees are considered the same if they are structurally identical, and the nodes have the same value.
constraints: The number of nodes in both trees is in the range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: Structurally identical with identical node values.
Different structure: left child vs right child.

commonMistakes: Comparing array serialization which might differ in trailing null representations
Not checking both null condition first
hints: If both nodes are null, return true.
If only one is null or values differ, return false.
Recursively check left and right subtrees.

problems.title: Symmetric Tree
problems.statement: Given the `root` of a binary tree, check whether it is a mirror of itself (i.e., symmetric around its center).
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 1000].

examples.explanation: 3 appears on outer left and outer right instead of mirrored.

commonMistakes: Comparing `t1.left` with `t2.left` instead of `t2.right` (symmetry requires mirror reflection)
Not comparing values when both nodes are non-null
hints: Two trees are mirrors if their roots have the same value, and right subtree of each is mirror of left subtree of the other.

problems.title: Path Sum
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, return `true` if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the values along the path equals `targetSum`.

A leaf is a node with no children.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5000].

examples.explanation: 1 is not a leaf, so path must continue to 2.

commonMistakes: Returning true when sum reaches target at a non-leaf node
Returning true for empty tree when targetSum === 0
hints: A valid path must terminate at a leaf (`node.left == null && node.right == null`).
Subtract `node.val` from `targetSum` as you descend the tree.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

problems.title: Path Sum II
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, return all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of the node values in the path equals `targetSum`.

Each path should be returned as a list of the node values, not node references.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5000].

examples.explanation: Root is a leaf and matches target.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to backtrack `currentPath.pop()`
Pushing reference `res.push(currentPath)` instead of shallow copy `res.push([...currentPath])`
hints: Backtracking: push current node to `path`, recurse into left/right, and pop node upon returning.
Clone the path array only when a leaf satisfying `targetSum` is reached.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=31 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=31 for complexity verification

problems.title: Binary Tree Paths
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return all root-to-leaf paths in any order.

A leaf is a node with no children.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 100].
commonMistakes: Appending arrow `->` after leaf nodes
Failing to check if a child is null before recursing
hints: Pass the accumulated string `current + node.val + '->'` to child calls.
When at a leaf, append `node.val` and push to result.

problems.title: Sum of Left Leaves
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the sum of all left leaves.

A leaf is a node with no children. A left leaf is a leaf that is the left child of another node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 1000].

examples.explanation: There are two left leaves in the binary tree, with values 9 and 15 respectively: 9 + 15 = 24.
Root is a leaf, but it is not a left leaf.
Node 4 is the only left leaf (5 is a right leaf, 2 is an internal node).
3 is the right child of 2, so there are no left leaves.

commonMistakes: Treating root as a left leaf
Counting internal left nodes that have children
hints: Pass a boolean flag `isLeft` to indicate if the current node was reached via a left edge.
If `!node.left && !node.right && isLeft`, add `node.val`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

problems.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
problems.statement:
Given a binary tree `root`, a node `X` in the tree is named good if in the path from the root to `X` there are no nodes with a value greater than `X`.

Return the number of good nodes in the binary tree.
constraints: The number of nodes in the binary tree is in the range [1, 10^5].

examples.explanation: Root Node (3) is always good. Node 4 -> (3,4) is good. Node 5 -> (3,4,5) is good. Node 3 -> (3,1,3) is good. Total 4.
Root is always a good node.
Only root 9 is good; other nodes are < 9.

commonMistakes: Initializing `maxSoFar` to 0 instead of `-Infinity` (failing on trees with all negative values)
Comparing with only the immediate parent instead of the maximum along the entire path from root
hints: Pass `maxVal` down the recursion representing the maximum value on the path from root.
If `node.val >= maxVal`, increment count and update `maxVal = max(maxVal, node.val)`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

problems.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter of the tree.

The diameter of a binary tree is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in a tree. This path may or may not pass through the root.

The length of a path between two nodes is represented by the number of edges between them.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].

examples.explanation: 3 is the length of the path [4,2,1,3] or [5,2,1,3].

commonMistakes: Assuming the diameter path must pass through the root
Counting nodes instead of edges (edges = nodes - 1)
hints: At each node, the longest path passing through it is `depth(left) + depth(right)`.
Update the global max diameter while returning `1 + max(depth(left), depth(right))`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Balanced Binary Tree
problems.statement:
Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced.

A height-balanced binary tree is a binary tree in which the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differs by more than one.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5000].

examples.explanation: Subtree heights differ by at most 1 at every node.
Subtrees of node 2 have heights 3 and 1, differing by 2.

commonMistakes: Recalculating depth repeatedly resulting in O(N^2) top-down check
Only checking balance at root while subtrees are unbalanced
hints: Compute depth bottom-up; return -1 immediately if any subtree is unbalanced.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Subtree of Another Tree
problems.statement:
Given the roots of two binary trees `root` and `subRoot`, return `true` if there is a subtree of `root` with the same structure and node values of `subRoot` and `false` otherwise.

A subtree of a binary tree `tree` is a tree that consists of a node in `tree` and all of this node's descendants. The tree `tree` could also be considered as a subtree of itself.
constraints: The number of nodes in the root tree is in the range [1, 2000].
The number of nodes in the subRoot tree is in the range [1, 1000].

examples.explanation: subRoot matches left subtree of root exactly.
Node 2 has a child 0 in root, but not in subRoot, so they are not identical.
Single node subRoot matches leaf node 1.

commonMistakes: Matching subRoot values inside an internal branch without ensuring subRoot covers all descendants to the leaves
String matching without unique node delimiters
hints: For each node in `root`, check if `isSameTree(node, subRoot)` is true.
Recursively test `dfs(node.left) || dfs(node.right)`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
problems.statement:
Given a binary search tree (BST), find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) node of two given nodes in the BST.

According to the definition of LCA on Wikipedia: “The lowest common ancestor is defined between two nodes `p` and `q` as the lowest node in `T` that has both `p` and `q` as descendants (where we allow a node to be a descendant of itself).”
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [2, 10^5].
p and q will exist in the BST.

examples.explanation: The LCA of nodes 2 and 8 is 6.
The LCA of nodes 2 and 4 is 2, since a node can be a descendant of itself.

commonMistakes: Traversing all branches O(N) instead of exploiting the BST order property O(H)
Returning the full node object instead of its value
hints: In a BST, if both `p` and `q` are smaller than `curr.val`, LCA must be in the left subtree.
If both are greater, LCA must be in the right subtree.
Otherwise, the current node is the split point and hence the LCA.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=11 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=7 for complexity verification

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
problems.statement:
Given a binary tree, find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes `p` and `q` in the tree.

According to the definition of LCA on Wikipedia: “The lowest common ancestor is defined between two nodes `p` and `q` as the lowest node in `T` that has both `p` and `q` as descendants (where we allow a node to be a descendant of itself).”
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [2, 10^5].
p and q will exist in the tree.

examples.explanation: The LCA of nodes 5 and 1 is 3.
The LCA of nodes 5 and 4 is 5, since a node can be a descendant of itself.

commonMistakes: Assuming the tree is a BST and using value comparisons
Not returning the found node when `node.val === p || node.val === q`
hints: Recursively search for `p` and `q` in left and right subtrees.
If both subtrees return non-null, current node is the LCA.
Otherwise, propagate whichever non-null subtree result was found.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.statement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST).

A valid BST is defined as follows:
- The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly less than the node's key.
- The right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly greater than the node's key.
- Both the left and right subtrees must also be binary search trees.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].

examples.explanation: Root node's value is 5 but its right child's left value is 3.
Duplicate values are not allowed in strict BST.

commonMistakes: Only comparing a node with its immediate left and right child (failing when a node in right subtree is smaller than root)
Allowing duplicate equal values (problem requires strictly less/greater)
Using 32-bit INT_MIN/INT_MAX as initial bounds instead of `-Infinity` / `Infinity`
hints: Pass valid bounds `(min, max)` down during recursion.
For left child: update `max = node.val`.
For right child: update `min = node.val`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.statement: Given the `root` of a binary search tree, and an integer `k`, return the `k-th` smallest value (1-indexed) of all the values of the nodes in the tree.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is n.

examples.explanation: Nodes in sorted order: [1,2,3,4,5,6]. 3rd smallest is 3.

commonMistakes: Traversing the entire tree when early exit upon `count === k` is possible
Using 0-indexing instead of 1-indexing
hints: Inorder traversal of a BST yields values in strictly ascending order.
Stop early as soon as the `k-th` node is visited.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification

problems.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums` where the elements are sorted in ascending order, convert it to a height-balanced binary search tree.

A height-balanced binary tree is a binary tree in which the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differs by more than one.
constraints: nums is sorted in a strictly increasing order.

examples.explanation: Pick middle element 0 as root, [-10, -3] as left subtree, [5, 9] as right subtree.
Pick 3 as root, 1 as left child (or 1 as root, 3 as right child).

commonMistakes: Slicing arrays repeatedly creating O(N log N) memory overhead
Picking off-center elements causing unbalanced tree
hints: The middle element of the sorted subarray must be the root of that subtree.
Recursively construct the left subtree from `nums[left..mid-1]` and right subtree from `nums[mid+1..right]`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=127 for complexity verification

problems.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problems.statement:
Serialization is the process of converting a data structure or object into a sequence of bits so that it can be stored in a file or memory buffer, or transmitted across a network connection link to be reconstructed later in the same or another computer environment.

Design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree. There is no restriction on how your serialization/deserialization algorithm should work. You just need to ensure that a binary tree can be serialized to a string and this string can be deserialized to the original tree structure.

Implement the `Codec` class:
- `Codec()` initializes the codec object.
- `string serialize((number | null)[] root)` serializes a tree to a single string.
- `(number | null)[] deserialize(string data)` deserializes your string back to the tree representation.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^4].

examples.explanation: Tree [1,2,3,null,null,4,5] serializes to string and deserializes back to original structure.
Empty tree serializes to empty string.

commonMistakes: Failing to parse 'null' strings back to literal null
Extra trailing commas corrupting deserialization
hints: Join array with commas for serialization.
Split by commas and convert numeric items back for deserialization.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=2 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=2 for complexity verification

problems.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
problems.statement: Given two integer arrays `preorder` and `inorder` where `preorder` is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and `inorder` is the inorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree in level-order array format.
constraints: preorder and inorder consist of unique values.
Each value of inorder also appears in preorder.
preorder is guaranteed to be the preorder traversal of the tree.
inorder is guaranteed to be the inorder traversal of the tree.

examples.explanation: Root is 3. In inorder, left of 3 is [9], right of 3 is [15,20,7].

commonMistakes: Using `inorder.indexOf` inside recursive calls causing O(N^2) time
Partitioning preorder boundaries incorrectly for left vs right subtree
hints: The first element of `preorder` is always the root.
Find the root index `mid` in `inorder` using a hash map.
Elements left of `mid` in `inorder` form the left subtree; elements to the right form the right subtree.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=63 for complexity verification
